title: The nightly metrics job
bridge: The nightly metrics job is like a scheduled report job in CI you know. A cron starts it, it calls APIs and it writes numbers somewhere. Except it writes time series with their own timestamps, so one run can fill in 12 weeks of history. And no series ever carries a person's name.
intro: Before agents start, we need numbers about how fcp delivers today: review wait, lead time, change failure and red-main time. This lesson builds the job that pulls those facts from GitHub and Jira every night and writes them to VictoriaMetrics. It also backfills the 12 weeks before October, the baseline every later number is compared with.

picture.caption: Every night at 02:20 one job reads GitHub and Jira, keeps the raw answer, and writes team-level weekly series.

steps.text: cron '20 2 * * *' starts the job at 02:20 UTC
asks for last week's PRs, commits, reviews and the unit-test runs on main
asks for RH tickets updated in the last 13 weeks
saves the raw answers as a JSON artifact of the run
computes weekly team numbers and posts Prometheus text with timestamps

sections.h: A cron at 02:20 and three source APIs
p: Open ai-agents/.github/workflows/delivery-metrics.yml, the file this lesson ends with. Its trigger is a cron, '20 2 * * *', so GitHub starts it at 02:20 UTC every night. Four steps run: actions/setup-node (Node 24, npm cache), then `npm ci --workspace metrics --include-workspace-root`. Then `npm run build -w shared -w metrics`, because metrics imports the shared package, and last `node metrics/dist/cli.js nightly`.

The job runs on ubuntu-22.04-2core, a GitHub-hosted runner, because it only calls public APIs. If G3 or G5 adds an ai-agents runner set by week 3, move it there. The code lives in a new npm workspace, ai-agents/metrics/, written in TypeScript on Node 24 with the global fetch.

The workspace has four source files and one command. src/github.ts pulls pull requests, src/ci.ts pulls unit-test runs on main, src/jira.ts pulls RH tickets, and src/vm.ts writes the numbers. src/cli.ts is the delivery-metrics command with two subcommands: nightly and backfill --weeks 12.

Every number we write is a point on a series: a name, a set of labels, a value and a timestamp. A series is the group of points with the same name and labels, for example delivery_merged_prs{team="frontend"}. Ours carry a team label and never a GitHub login; teams under 3 people report as 'other'.

callout.text: GitHub reads use a separate read-only App (pull requests, contents, actions and checks: read) through actions/create-github-app-token. The rhino-ai-agents key stays with the broker alone, as in lesson p2-4.

p: GraphQL is GitHub's second API: you POST one query text and name exactly the fields you want back. One request returns PRs, their commits and their review events together, where REST would need three calls per PR. The small helper graphql in src/gh.ts does the POST to https://api.github.com/graphql with the App token.
This block is lines 2 to 19 of the sketch; we drop only the file-path comment on line 1. Part 2 holds the function that runs the query.
sections.because: We ask GitHub for everything in one query, because all three delivery metrics start from the same PR data.

notes.text: What this file is for: the facts about each PR that the metrics in compute.ts need.
graphql(query, variables) posts to GitHub's GraphQL endpoint with the read-only App token; it lives in src/gh.ts.
PrSearch is the TypeScript shape of the answer, so the code in part 2 is typed.
The query text as a template literal; $q and $after are variables filled in per call.
search is GitHub's search API: $q is the search text, ISSUE covers issues and PRs, 50 items per page.
pageInfo says whether there is another page and gives the cursor to ask for it.
Per PR: number, when it opened, when it merged, the body text and the author login (used only to find a team).
Up to 100 commits with their authored date and message; the oldest date is where lead time starts.
Two kinds of timeline events only: the moment a draft became ready, and each review.
__typename names the kind of each event, so compute.ts can tell them apart.
A review carries its state, time and author. The author's __typename says User or Bot, so Byte's reviews never count as a person.

p: GitHub search stops at 1000 results, so pullRequests asks for one week at a time. An async generator is a function declared with `async function*`. It yields values one at a time while it still fetches, and the caller reads it with `for await`. A cursor is the bookmark string GitHub gives you to ask for the next page.
This block is lines 21 to 35 of the sketch, unchanged.
sections.because: We follow the cursor to every page, because one week of fcp PRs can be more than 50.

notes.text: The week-per-query rule; the job calls this twice, once by created date and once by merged date.
The function takes the repo, the week's start and end dates, and which date field to search by.
The search text, for example repo:RhinoHealth/fcp is:pr created:2026-09-01..2026-09-07.
after is the cursor; null means the first page.
One POST; the answer is typed as PrSearch and we take its search part.
For each PR we pull commits and timelineItems apart from the rest; ...pr keeps the plain fields.
ISO date strings sort as text in time order, so [0] is the oldest commit. A PR with no commits falls back to createdAt.
aiTrailer is true when the body says 'Generated with Claude Code' or a commit carries the Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer. This feeds 'share of PRs with AI help'.
yield hands one PR to the caller right away, with the two computed fields and the timeline events.
If GitHub says there is another page, keep its cursor; otherwise null ends the loop.
do...while runs the body at least once, then repeats while a cursor remains.

callout.text: To test this without GitHub, swap src/gh.ts for a stub that returns pages from an array. The lab does exactly that.

sections.h: ci.ts part 1: only the required jobs count
p: Red-main time is the number of hours fcp's main branch has a failing required check. We read it from the GitHub Actions REST API, not GraphQL, because runs and jobs are REST resources. The helpers rest and restPages in src/gh.ts do the fetch; restPages follows the Link: next header until the last page.

Only the required unit-test jobs count. The integration-test jobs are flaky and they are G7's problem, so counting them would paint main red for the wrong reason. This block is lines 2 to 22 of the sketch; only the file-path comment is dropped.
sections.because: We read only the three required unit-test jobs, because flaky integration tests would make main look red when the code is fine.

notes.text: REQUIRED maps each workflow file to the job names that count; Record<string, string[]> means string keys to string arrays.
Two names per workflow: the new name after G0's rename, and the old name 'Unit Tests' for earlier runs.
A Result is one finished job: which workflow, when it finished, and whether it passed.
mainResults is an async generator again; since is the date to start from, for example 13 weeks back.
The query asks only for completed runs on main created on or after since.
restPages lists one workflow file's runs, page by page, from /repos/{repo}/actions/workflows/{file}/runs.
Each run has jobs; one more REST call lists them.
Find the job whose name is in our list; other jobs in the run are ignored.
Keep only success or failure; cancelled or skipped jobs say nothing about main.
Yield the result with a real Date, so part 2 can sort and subtract times.

sections.h: ci.ts part 2: overlapping red windows count once
p: Main is red while any required job's latest result is a failure. If cloud is red from 00:00 to 02:00 and client from 01:00 to 03:00, main was red for 3 hours, not 4. redHours walks the results in time order and keeps one state per workflow. This block is lines 24 to 35 of the sketch.
sections.because: We keep one boolean per workflow and time when any is false, because overlapping red windows must count once.

notes.text: A pure function: results in, hours out, so a node:test can check it with a fixture and no network.
state remembers the latest result per workflow file: true for green, false for red.
redSince is the time main turned red, or undefined while it is green; total adds up the hours.
toSorted returns a sorted copy (Node 20 and later), oldest result first, without changing the input.
Record this workflow's latest result.
Main is red now if any workflow's latest result is false.
Green to red: remember when it happened.
Red to green: add the window's length in hours (milliseconds divided by 3,600,000) and clear redSince.
The answer in hours for the whole window of results you passed in.

callout.text: A window still red at the last result is not counted, because nothing closes it. When the nightly job computes a week, pass in the results up to the end of that week. On a red day, check the last state by hand.

sections.h: compute.ts part 1: three numbers per PR
p: compute.ts turns the pulled data into numbers, weekly and per team. Nothing in it is ever written per person. Each metric is one small function: a PullRequest in, hours out, or undefined when the PR has no such event yet.

Review wait starts when the PR became ready for review, or when it opened if it was never a draft. It ends at the first review by a person other than the author. Lead time runs from the first commit to the merge.

A change failed when a revert, hotfix or Bug fix touches its lines within 14 days. G2's golden-set miner finds those fixes. This block is lines 2 to 18 of the sketch; only the file-path comment is dropped.
sections.because: We write one small pure function per metric, because each can be tested on a fixture and read in a minute.

notes.text: stats.ts holds the maths: hours and days between two ISO timestamps, median, and quantile like Python's statistics module.
The data shapes come from types.ts; MergedPr is a PullRequest whose mergedAt is not null.
reviewWaitHours returns a number or undefined, so a PR with no review yet is left out, not counted as 0.
The ready time: the ReadyForReviewEvent if there was one, else the moment the PR opened.
The first review that is by a User (not a Bot such as Byte) and not by the author.
If there was a review, the hours between; otherwise undefined.
Lead time: first commit to merge, only for merged PRs.
changeFailed takes the PR and the list of fixes from G2's miner.
True when a fix says this PR number introduced the bug and the fix merged within 14 days of the PR.

sections.h: compute.ts part 2: weekly points per team
p: A Point is what vm.ts writes: a series name, its labels, a value and the week's timestamp. weeklyPoints groups the week's PRs by team and yields one Point per number. p50 is the median: half the values are below it.

p85 is the value that 85% of the values sit below. With it the dashboard shows the slow tail, not only the middle. This block is lines 20 to 35 of the sketch, unchanged. Lead time, red-main hours and the agent metrics follow the same pattern in the real file; the sketch shows three.
sections.because: We emit p50, p85 and counts per team, because weekly numbers for about 25 engineers are noisy and one average misleads.

notes.text: teamOf maps a PR to a team name; the login lookup from teams.ts happens inside it. weekTs is the week's timestamp in milliseconds.
A Map from team to that team's PRs for this week.
The comment is the rule: an agent PR counts for the requester's team, and a team under 3 people is 'other'.
Append the PR to its team's list; the spread copies the old list plus the new PR.
All review waits that exist; filter drops the undefined ones.
With fewer than 2 values a median says nothing, so the team gets no review-wait point that week.
Yield the p50 point: name, the labels team and q, the median, the timestamp.
Same series, label q=p85, the 0.85 quantile.
merged narrows the type: the (p): p is MergedPr predicate tells TypeScript that mergedAt is set.
How many PRs merged this week; the dashboard shows it only next to change failure.
How many of those failed within 14 days; the dashboard divides this by merged PRs.

sections.h: Jira, the writer and the 12-week backfill
p: src/jira.ts uses Jira REST v3 through the small fetch client in shared/src/jira.ts (lesson p9-2). It runs the JQL `project = RH AND updated >= -13w` against rhino-fcp.atlassian.net with a read-only service account token. The token sits in Vault at kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/jira-metrics. It keeps the key, the type, status changes, the Nova assignee flag and the PR keys from titles; no names are stored.

src/vm.ts writes Prometheus text, one line per Point, with a millisecond timestamp at the end of each line. The timestamp is what puts a backfilled point on the right day. It posts to the integration VMUser the way infrastructure's send-workflow-result.yml does. The secret integration-metrics-user comes from Secrets Manager through the GitHubActions OIDC role; confirm with DevOps that this role trusts RhinoHealth/ai-agents.

Each night the job also stores the raw pull as a JSON artifact of the workflow run. When a metric has a bug, you fix compute.ts and recompute from the artifact without calling the APIs again. Backfill means computing past weeks from history: `delivery-metrics backfill --weeks 12 --until 2026-09-30` writes the 12 weeks before October as delivery_baseline_* series. Check three numbers by hand against GitHub before you trust it.

A cohort is a group you compare with another: agent PRs against human PRs, or agent-eligible tickets by G4's Jira label. Agent-only metrics start as 'no data', not 0, so charts show no fake drop. Byte's two rates (G2) and G3's stuck loops and clean endings get delivery_* names too, so one dashboard holds all seventeen.

callout.text: Aggregate before writing: a login is used in memory to find the team and is then dropped. Series carry team, never login.

quiz.q: Why does pullRequests search one week at a time?

options.text: GitHub search returns at most 1000 results, so a narrow window keeps every PR in reach.
options.why: The comment on the function says it: one week per query, run again by merged date.

options.text: The App token expires after one hour, so each week needs a fresh token.
options.why: Tokens do expire after an hour, but many weeks fit in that time; the limit is the search cap.

options.text: VictoriaMetrics accepts only one week of points per write.
options.why: The writer takes any timestamps; backfill writes 12 weeks in one run.

quiz.q: cloud-ci.yml is red from 00:00 to 02:00 and client-ci.yml from 01:00 to 03:00. What does redHours return?

options.text: 4, because each workflow was red for 2 hours.
options.why: Adding the windows counts the shared hour twice; main was red once.

options.text: 3, because main is red while any required job is red.
options.why: One state per workflow: main turned red at 00:00 and green at 03:00.

options.text: 2, the longer of the two windows.
options.why: The windows overlap but neither sits inside the other; the union is 3 hours.

quiz.q: A team has two engineers. How does their work appear in the series?

options.text: Under their GitHub logins, so the numbers stay exact.
options.why: No series carries a login; that is the wall this job keeps.

options.text: It is skipped, because two values make no median.
options.why: Only the review-wait median needs 2 values; the PRs still count, under 'other'.

options.text: Under team='other', together with every other team under 3 people.
options.why: Teams under 3 people report as 'other', so a number never points at one person.

words.plain: The points that share one name and one set of labels over time; ours carry team, never a login.
A function declared async function* that yields values one at a time while it still fetches; read it with for await.
The bookmark string GitHub returns with a page, which you send back to get the next page.
Hours during which any required unit-test job on main has a failing latest result; overlaps count once.
The value that 85% of the week's values sit below; shown next to p50, the median.
Computing past weeks from history and writing them with their own timestamps, so the baseline exists before agents start.
A group you compare with another, such as agent PRs against human PRs.
